question:
A 10-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with his parents. The boy complains of fever, neck stiffness, and drowsiness for the last several days. His past medical history is noncontributory. The boy was born at 39 weeks gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery. He is up to date on all vaccines and is meeting all developmental milestones. There were no sick contacts at home or at school. The family did not travel out of the area recently. His heart rate is 100/min, respiratory rate is 22/min, blood pressure is 105/65 mm Hg, and temperature is 40.5ºC (104.9°F). On physical examination, he appears unwell and confused. His heart rate is elevated with a regular rhythm and his lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. During the examination, he experiences a right-sided focal seizure, which is controlled with lorazepam. A head CT reveals bilateral asymmetrical hypodensities of the temporal region. A lumbar puncture is performed and reveals the following:
WBC count 25/mm3
Cell predominance lymphocytes
Protein elevated
The patient is started on a medication to treat the underlying cause of his symptoms. What is the mechanism of action of this medication?

options.opb: Binding with ergosterol in the cell membrane

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Fever, neck stiffness, drowsiness" -> "Suspicion of meningitis" -> "Lumbar puncture performed" -> "CSF analysis shows elevated protein and lymphocytic predominance" -> "Likely viral or aseptic meningitis" -> "Treatment initiated based on suspected etiology" -> 80%
enhanced_information: The patient presents with symptoms suggestive of meningitis, confirmed by CSF analysis showing elevated protein and lymphocytic predominance. The likely etiology is viral or aseptic meningitis. The treatment initiated is based on suspected viral meningitis. The mechanism of action of the medication is likely related to viral meningitis treatment.
analysis: The patient is presenting with symptoms suggestive of viral or aseptic meningitis, as indicated by the CSF analysis showing elevated protein and lymphocytic predominance. The treatment initiated is likely targeting the viral etiology. In viral meningitis, the mainstay of treatment involves supportive care and antiviral medications. Among the given options, nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibition (opd) is the mechanism of action commonly associated with antiviral medications used to treat viral infections like meningitis caused by certain viruses. This option aligns with the context provided.
